name: Wei Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wei. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, happy to. I think about this stuff a lot, so you might have to stop me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a carpenter for Halden Construction on a hospital extension, a big commercial job. I do door frames, ceiling grids, timber partitions and a lot of first fix, which is the structural timber before plastering. I'm on site at seven and I use an AI app on my phone to check the drawings and plan which rooms I'll finish that day. I like the big team and the order of a big site, but the pay is lower than on the city jobs and the travel's long.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's your life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Ana, who's a hairdresser, and we're saving to get married, or trying to. I've just bought a used van because I want to start my own small building firm in a year or two, and that took nearly all our savings. There aren't many contractors round here, so if Halden doesn't have work, I'd have to go out on my own sooner. We go to church most Sundays with Ana's parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So AI is a handy app and nothing more. That's basically how I use it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool for people who use it, and nothing to be scared of. I'd tell the guys on site to try it for planning their day. Online I'd probably say the real changes come from hard work and small businesses, not tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI isn't the problem. The hospital contract ends in eight months, and I've spent my savings on a van for the firm I haven't started yet. So this picture is about my own nerve, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start doing small kitchen and bathroom jobs at weekends with the van, to build up customers before Halden finishes. I'd use AI to write the quotes and keep the books. And I'd cut back, no eating out, until we've got a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, and a bit nervous. Mostly about money, not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ana say about the weekend work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say don't wear yourself out, and she'd be right. But she also believes in it, her dad ran his own garage for thirty years. She'd probably do my bookings if the AI didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Halden's contract ends and the weekend work isn't enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go full time on my own and take every small job going, fences, decks, doors. It would be tight for a few months. I'd rather do that than drive two hours to the city every day.

say: AI is a **good tool** for people who use it, and nothing to fear.
Real change comes from **hard work** and **small businesses**, not technology.
think: The **hospital contract** ends in eight months.
He's spent his **savings** on a van for a firm not yet started.
do: Do weekend **kitchen and bathroom** jobs to build customers.
Use AI to write **quotes** and keep the **books**.
Stop eating out until they have **a month** saved.
feel: **Excited** and a bit **nervous**, mostly about money.
S0.quote: The hospital contract ends in eight months, and I've spent my savings on a van for the firm I haven't started yet.
fieldNote: AI isn't the issue; a **contract ending** and spent savings are, so **uneasy**.
Entrepreneurial and **risk-comfortable**, with family examples of self-employment.
Already uses AI **daily** for planning and drawings.

steps.text: Fit kitchens and bathrooms at weekends with the new van
Use AI to write quotes and keep the books
Stop eating out until a month's costs are saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one I actually expect. The office side changes, the hands side later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who want to work for themselves. Big firms lose their advantage when software does the paperwork for everyone. I'd say government should keep out of the way and let people get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI doing the quotes, invoices and ordering means a one-man building firm can look like a five-man firm from day one. The risk is that everyone thinks the same and the market fills up with one-man firms undercutting each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd register the business in the first six months and use AI for quotes, invoices and ordering timber. I'd do a short course on running a building business, contracts and tax. I'd keep a day or two a week at Halden for steady money as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. A little nervous about the competition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Halden would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The site office people, the woman who does the orders and the estimator. They're good at what they do, but software does that now in this picture. I'd offer one of them work doing my paperwork, but I couldn't pay much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With thin savings, isn't starting a firm risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very risky. But staying put is risky too, because Halden's work ends anyway. At least this way I own the risk.

say: This picture is a **chance** for people who want to **work for themselves**.
Government should **keep out** of the way and let people get on with it.
think: AI makes a **one-man firm** look like five from day one.
Too many small firms could end up **undercutting** each other.
do: **Register the business** in the first six months.
Take a short course on **contracts and tax** for builders.
Keep a day or two a week at **Halden** for steady money.
S1.quote: AI doing the quotes, invoices and ordering means a one-man building firm can look like a five-man firm from day one.
fieldNote: Sees Steady Disruption as an **opportunity**, but thin savings keep him **uneasy**.
Free-market view: **own the risk** rather than wait.
Feels for Halden's **office staff**, whose tasks go first.

steps.text: Register his own building firm within six months
Run quotes, invoices and timber orders through AI
Take a short course on building contracts and tax

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for AGI, then robots for hands-on work by 2031. That's fast, even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get in early and own the tools, don't wait for someone else to look after you. Families should stick together and help each other start things. I wouldn't want a big government scheme telling people what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2031 I either own the robots or I compete with them, and with no savings I'm not sure which side I'll land on. The thinking side of a firm goes in 2028, which helps me, but my hands are worth a lot less after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the firm right away, not in a year, and use AI for everything that isn't hammer and saw. I'd ask Ana's dad about a small family loan to save toward buying or leasing a building robot by 2031. I'd also learn how those robots get set up and repaired, because that work might last longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, really. Excited too, but nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens between 2028 and 2031 for your firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those are the money years. Everyone would want building done before the robots change prices, so I'd take every job and save hard. If I haven't got a cushion by 2031, I'm just another guy with a van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a loan from Ana's dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I could pay it back properly, with a written plan. He'd respect that. Family should help, but it shouldn't be a gift.

say: People should get in early and **own the tools**.
Families should **stick together** and help each other start things, without big schemes.
think: By **2031** he either owns the robots or **competes** with them.
AGI helps his office side, but his **hands** lose value after 2031.
do: Start the **firm** immediately, with AI for all admin.
Ask Ana's dad for a **family loan** toward a building robot.
Learn how building robots are **set up and repaired**.
S2.quote: By 2031 I either own the robots or I compete with them, and with no savings I'm not sure which side I'll land on.
fieldNote: Adaptive and confident, but **no savings** make the race to 2031 risky: **anxious**.
Wants **family support** as a loan, not a gift.

steps.text: Start his building firm straight away with the van
Borrow from Ana's dad toward leasing a building robot
Learn how building robots are set up and repaired
Use AI for every office task in the firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So 2031 for the thinking side and robots by 2034. That suits me better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift for anyone willing to work. Learn a trade, start something, don't wait for help. I'd say it at church and on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to build a small firm with AI doing the office work, then buy the robots when they turn up in 2034. I'd be 34, maybe married with a child. The risk is that big firms buy robots first and squeeze the small ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a few days at Halden while building up the firm over two years. I'd save hard, aiming for three months in the bank by 2028. And I'd learn everything I could about building robots as they start appearing on big sites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. Uneasy about the big firms, but hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you compete if the big firms get robots first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small jobs, kitchens, extensions, people's homes. Big firms with robots want big repeat jobs, hospitals and estates. I'd go where they don't bother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ana about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd marry next year and wait a bit for children until the firm is steady. She'd agree, I think. Her parents would want grandchildren sooner, but they'd understand.

People should start something and **not wait** for help.

fieldNote: Five years matches his plan, so the outlook is **hopeful**, though money keeps him **uneasy**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, 2036 and 2039. That's a proper runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best-case picture for anyone who's prepared to work. Ten years is enough to build a business from nothing. I'd say people shouldn't wait for the government to plan their lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is enough to build something my children could take over, and I'd rather own a firm than be a number on a site list. I'd want my own crew and some machines by 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry Ana, start the firm next year and grow it steadily, maybe hire one apprentice by year three. I'd save and invest in better tools first, then machines later. I'd use AI for every bit of admin and design.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit uneasy about money in the first year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's how I learned, from an old carpenter called Joe who took a chance on me. I'd want to do the same. And a young person learns the new machines faster than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that could knock you off course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An injury, or a quiet year with no work. With almost nothing saved, one bad winter would hurt. That's the real risk, not the robots.

Ten years is enough to **build a business** from nothing.
People shouldn't wait for **government** to plan their lives.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots come before I've built anything up and I'd be stuck with a van and a loan. What would help is cheap business loans and lower tax for small firms in their first years, so people like me can buy the machines instead of being replaced by them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who wants to take the risk. Nobody is going to hand me a future. I'd rather borrow, build and take the risk than wait for someone to save me.

headlineQuote: Nobody is going to hand me a future. I'd rather borrow, build and take the risk than wait for someone to save me.
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old carpenter** on a hospital extension for a commercial contractor.
He uses **AI daily** and has spent his savings on a van to start his **own firm**.
He lives with Ana, a hairdresser, and leans on **family and church**, not government.
He sees AI taking office work as a **chance** for small firms to compete.
His mood stays **uneasy**, rising to **anxious** only when robots arrive by 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would arrive before his firm has any **savings**.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap business loans** and lower tax for new small firms.
